name: Rafael Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI firms, employers, unions, political parties and government; we don't sell or campaign. Your answers are confidential, including the parts you wouldn't say at work. What is a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage five claims leads at a large insurer. When a roof leaks, one estimate may say patch and another says replace; my team checks photographs, repair prices and the policy before a letter goes out. I've worked claims for nineteen years, have an MBA and am one of the stronger people here on difficult damage disputes. I have never used an AI tool; I like the original photograph beside the estimate.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is waiting for you at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and live with my partner Amira and our children, six and twelve, in a mortgaged house. Amira works hospital shifts in patient care. My manager pay is about typical, we have four months of expenses saved, and there are a few other insurer offices nearby. The older child has a school trip coming up; I watch the cash before agreeing to a big home project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the software stays small, our claims desk will still have people settling arguments over storm damage. I have a manager's wage at the usual level and four months of expenses saved. Amira's hospital shifts and mine pay the mortgage, though a second roof leak would use that cushion quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my claims leads to keep the original repair photographs with every settlement letter. I'd tell Amira that a modest writing helper does not change who signs a decision. I would not send a claimant a letter I have not read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I trust my judgment on difficult claims, and there are a few other insurer offices in reach if ours closes a team. I have never used AI; I prefer seeing the old estimate and the new one side by side. At home I feel we can manage the mortgage if both wages keep coming, though four months is not endless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next week I'll review the eight roof claims whose first estimates were overturned and have each lead attach the repair photograph to the decision. Through the first year of a plateau I'll keep the same sign-off practice and put 90 a month into cash only while our mortgage, food and school costs are paid. I won't buy a new claims tool with my own money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my job in this picture. I still get annoyed when a neat letter hides a missing photograph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why were those eight estimates changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One contractor priced a whole roof when only a small section had water damage; another missed soaked insulation. We caught both by looking at the images and calling the household. A roof is not repaired by agreeing on a nicer paragraph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does four months saved mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we could take time to find work, not that we can stop checking bills. Our children are six and twelve, and the older one needs a school trip payment soon. I would stop the 90 transfer if an ordinary bill needed it.

I'd tell Amira I would read every **claimant letter** before signing.
think: My **judgment and nearby insurers** make this job feel secure in a mild-change world.
Four months saved is useful, while **our mortgage** remains manageable only if both wages continue.

Keep **photographs beside decisions** in the first plateau year.
Save **90 monthly** only after mortgage, food and school costs are paid.
feel: I feel **calm** about my work, though poor evidence still irritates me.

Save 90 monthly only after mortgage, food and school costs are paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing settlement letters, checking estimates, pricing work and answering customers fill most of our day. A stronger tool could draft all that and leave fewer claims leads. A person may still walk a damaged house, but most of my manager job is judgment on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the director for a list of which claim decisions the system can make and which a named worker must approve. I'd tell claimants to keep a way to dispute a refused repair. I'd want an old-claim test before a live settlement changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose the team lead layer if one manager oversees twice as many automated files. I am good at this work, but I have not used AI and don't want to pretend a short demo would qualify me to check it. Amira's hospital pay helps, yet four months would not last through a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January I'll request a paid demonstration using twenty closed roof claims, with the claims auditor beside me and the director's approval. If it catches the missed insulation, I'll ask for paid instruction on the review screen; I won't approve live automatic denials without the auditor and director signing off. I'll check posted manager roles at the two reachable insurers and apply where the wage and hours cover our bills, leaving my present pay only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own role. I can ask for a fair test, but I cannot promise the company will keep a manager for every file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a failed test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it calls the wet insulation dry because the first estimate did, I would take the original photo to the auditor. The insurer can repair a wrong model, but the household still has a damp room. A trial on tidy files would tell us nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let a colleague teach you the screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if it is paid time and the auditor can show me where each number came from. I am slow to start new tools, not unwilling to check a claim. I still won't use an automatic denial until the right people approve it.

say: I'd demand a **named human approver** for refused repairs.
I'd ask for **closed-claim testing** before live settlements change.
think: My **team lead layer** could disappear despite my claims skill.
A **short AI demonstration** would not qualify me to check a new claims system.
do: Request a **paid twenty-claim demonstration** with auditor and director approval.
Learn the **review screen** only after a successful old-claim test, offered paid instruction and auditor source tracing.
Apply for **posted insurer roles** with viable pay; leave only after a signed offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my job and the household search time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI in 2028 could read the roof photographs, compare contractor prices and settle nearly every claim better and cheaper than my desk. Amira's hospital care is hands-on for now, though its notes and schedules change in 2028 and capable robots follow around 2031. Walking a wet house is physical, but judging the damage is still thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the claims staff the 2028 date and ask for written notice terms. I'd tell Amira not to commit to the planned garden extension this winter. I would ask the insurer for real paid field openings rather than a course brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my manager post to end, even if I am one of the best at difficult roofs. Four months saved and Amira's current hospital pay might hold the mortgage briefly, but losing my wage would keep me awake. I am not counting on a field assessor job staying intact when AGI can judge the photographs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask the field supervisor whether any posted paid site-inspection openings exist and what safety certification is required; I won't claim the job is mine. If the company funds the certificate on paid time and arranges supervised visits, I'll complete it only if Amira or another agreed adult can cover school pickup. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my desk ends, I'll apply for posted field work only if its wage with Amira's confirmed hours covers mortgage, food and school costs; otherwise we'll postpone the garden-extension deposit and ask the lender about terms before arrears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I can draw a plan, but four months of cash is short when a full manager wage disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of a field visit would still need you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lift a loose tile, measure a wet wall and take photographs with a trained assessor. The decision and report could be done by AGI in 2028; capable robots can do the physical visit around 2031. A ladder is not a safe job merely because a computer cannot climb it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the children hear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would be eight and fourteen. I'd say the garden extension is delayed and school stays paid first. I would not ask them to measure the family bank balance.

I'd ask for **posted paid field work**, not a course promise.
think: I expect my **manager wage to end** by 2028.
Four months cash and Amira's pay may not cover a **long search**.
do: Ask about **posted field openings** and safety requirements this month.
Complete a **funded paid-time certificate** only with supervised visits and agreed school pickup.
Apply for **posted field work** only if combined confirmed wages cover family bills.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing my wage despite four months saved.
S2.quote: A ladder is not a safe job merely because a computer cannot climb it yet.

Field visits need **safety training and supervision**; their reports face AGI immediately.
The garden extension is delayed before a deposit if **wages cannot cover bills**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I could observe a real inspection before making a decision. Claims judgment faces AGI in 2031; physical roof visits may last until capable robots arrive around 2034, but their reports and prices change first. I need to compare that short bridge with staying in management as long as the salary arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company to publish actual paid site posts and the required training hours. I'd tell Amira we should keep four months in cash rather than put it all against the mortgage. I'd tell the children their school plans come before a garden extension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could earn in inspections if a paid position appears, but I would start as a supervised learner. My current typical manager pay is safer than a guessed inspection wage. Five years gives us room to reduce debt, though I can't know what the insurer will post in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'll ask for four paid shadow visits with the field team and take them only with supervisor approval, safety instruction and school pickup covered. I'll add 120 a month to our mortgage payment while preserving four months cash and paying school costs, stopping if Amira's confirmed shifts fall. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'll take a posted site role only if its wage plus Amira's pay covers mortgage, food and school costs; otherwise I'll search other insurers before spending our reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though five years gives me a chance to test the ladder and the wage. I would rather find out in daylight than in a redundancy meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens on a shadow visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the ladder footing and measure a damaged ceiling under the assessor's eye. I can read a contractor's estimate, but I cannot claim I know field safety from an MBA. Wet plaster does not care what degree is on my wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Amira loses shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra 120 mortgage payment stops. We keep the four months of cash and pay the usual mortgage from confirmed wages. I would not turn a buffer into home equity just before income changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'll be 53, our younger child sixteen and our older one twenty-two. I can't assume either child's income pays our mortgage. Claims decisions face AGI in 2036 and capable robots could do site visits around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the insurer to make a written plan for human review and paid learning posts. I'd tell Amira we should keep checking the mortgage balance and the cash reserve each year. I would tell claimants how to dispute a refusal, whichever system wrote it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years could let me reach six months cash and reduce debt if both paychecks continue. I would still expect my claims-manager job to change or end at AGI, and a field role would be temporary if robots arrive. I don't want to leave a familiar wage for a future post that no one has funded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next year I'll request a paid safety course linked to real site visits and enroll only if the field supervisor approves, the company pays the fee and work hours, and pickup is arranged. I'll save 140 monthly toward six months cash after mortgage and school bills while both wages hold, reviewing the amount each year. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'll apply for posted field work only if trained and its wage with Amira's confirmed pay covers our bills; I would leave only for a signed offer and keep searching if none pays enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the desk ending in a decade, but the time gives us choices. I do not need to spend our four months in cash to prove I am adaptable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the children to help then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The younger might still be in school at sixteen, and the older may live elsewhere at twenty-two. I would not count either wage. We should make our own mortgage plan while we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the safety course worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A safety course needs a paid site shift and a named supervisor, not a certificate left in a drawer. The course fee and my hours need company funding; family pickup needs a real answer. I have not used AI, and I will not pretend that alone protects my desk.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I expect my claims-manager wage to end, and four months cash is short for a family mortgage even with Amira working. Written notice, paid safety learning tied to a real site post and a wage we can live on would help. I would want a named human route for a household to challenge a wrong refusal.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the household what a delayed claim does to a damp child's bedroom. I can read three estimates in ten minutes, but someone has to answer when the ceiling stains again. A claim number is not a dry room.

headlineQuote: A claim number is not a dry room.
portrait: Rafael, **43**, leads five insurer claims managers and holds an MBA after nineteen years in damage disputes.
He has never used AI, but his **roof-claim expertise** makes him strong at reading estimates against photographs.
Typical manager pay, **four months cash**, Amira's hospital shifts and a mortgage support their two school-age children.
He seeks **paid supervised field learning** while recognizing AGI can judge site photographs and robots can visit later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his claims-manager wage before a family mortgage is safe.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written notice** and funded safety learning tied to an actual paid site post.
He wants an **affordable wage** and a human route to challenge wrong claim refusals.
